Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given an orthogonal basis [MATH: \mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_n\}] of [MATH: S=\textrm{Span}\{\mathcal{B}\},] there is an easy way to find the components of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}\in S] with respect to this basis. The vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] with respect to the basis [MATH: \mathcal{B}] is
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; ⋮; x_{n}]]

Content:
Furthermore, if the basis is orthonormal, then we know that [MATH: \mathbf{q}_i\cdot\mathbf{q}_i=1]. So, the formula for each component is
[MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; ⋮; x_{n}]]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of [MATH: \mathcal{B}] as [MATH: \mathbf{q}_1,\, \mathbf{q}_2,\,\mathbf{q}_3.]

Since [MATH: \mathcal{B}] is an orthogonal basis, we have that [MATH: [x_{1}; x_{2}; x_{3}]] where [MATH: x_i = \dfrac{\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{q}_i}{\mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{q}_i}.]

Computing [MATH: x_2,] we obtain

[MATH: x_{2}|= (x ⋅ q_{2})/(q_{2} ⋅ q_{2}); = (4 ⋅ 1 + 6 ⋅ 1 + (− 2) ⋅ (− 4))/(1^{2} + 1^{2} + (− 4)^{2}); = (4 + 6 + 8)/(1 + 1 + 16); = 1.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: The Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem

Content:
Given any vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}] and any subspace [MATH: W] in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n,] we can always write [MATH: \mathbf{x}] as a sum of a vector from [MATH: W] and a vector from [MATH: W^{\perp}.] This fact is known as the orthogonal decomposition theorem. We can state it formally as follows:

Content:
> Let [MATH: W] be a subspace of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n.] Then each [MATH: \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n] can be written uniquely in the form
> [MATH: \mathbf{x}= \mathbf{y}+\mathbf{z}]
> where [MATH: \mathbf{y} \in W] and [MATH: \mathbf{z} \in W^{\perp}.]

Content:
> Moreover, since [MATH: \mathbf y] is the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf x] onto the subspace [MATH: W,] if [MATH: \{\mathbf{u}_1\,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}] is any orthogonal basis of [MATH: W,] then
> [MATH: y|= proj_{W}x; = proj_{u_{1}}x + proj_{u_{2}}x + ⋯ + proj_{u_{p}}x; = (x ⋅ u_{1})/(u_{1} ⋅ u_{1})u_{1} + (x ⋅ u_{2})/(u_{2} ⋅ u_{2})u_{2} + ⋯ + (x ⋅ u_{p})/(u_{p} ⋅ u_{p})u_{p}.]
